messages.subject: Predicting with a rw2 + besag kronecker product model
messages.subject_clean: Predicting with a rw2 + besag kronecker product model
messages.body_plain:
I have a spatio-temporal data set and want to fit a rw2 + besag kronecker product model, and use it to make predictions. For testing I started with an rw2 group iid model:

 inla(formula = Y ~ -1 + f(i_week, model='rw2', constr=FALSE,
                                             group=i_lad, control.group=list(model='iid')),
        data = d,
        family='binomial', Ntrials=d$n,
        control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE, link=1))

All data in the last week are NA and so are predicted by extrapolating the RW2 (hence the constr=FALSE). The results look as expected:

Then I swapped out 'iid' for 'besag', to borrow strength from spatial neighbors, as in:

inla(formula = Y ~ -1 + f(i_week, model='rw2', constr=FALSE,
                                             group=i_lad,
                                             control.group=list(model='besag', graph=lad_adj)),
        data = d,
        family='binomial', Ntrials=d$n,
        control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE, link=1))

The results change dramatically, and not in a good way:

I think this has to do with the sum-to-zero constraint in the besag model. If so, is there any way to turn the constraint off inside control.group? (I tried control.group(..., constr=FALSE) but that didn't work.)

Any suggestions are welcome - many thanks in advance!

messages.subject: Threshold-like behaviour with pc priors in SPDE model ?
messages.subject_clean: Threshold-like behaviour with pc priors in SPDE model ?
messages.body_plain:
Hello INLA people

I have been using INLA for spatial models for a little while and I often have had the impression that my choices of pc priors had very little impacts on the estimation of the hyperparameters of the spatial field when using SPDE model. Often, I have to use extreme priors to significantly change the estimation of hyperparameters. This could be due to the amount of data overwhelming the priors, but in most cases I have few data and the estimation of parameters such as the range or the sd of the spatial field should at least be moderatly influenced by the priors and associated with relatively large uncertainties.

I'm currently trying to build spatiotemporal models for zero-inflated seasonal count data using a negative binomial distribution and an SPDE model with an AR1 weekly component. In some cases, I'm suspecting confounding between the weekly spatial fields and a temporal fixed effect used to capture the seasonal trend within seasons (julian date with a quadratic effect). The weekly spatial field sometimes takes up what should be attributed to the julian date. One of the possible solution to prevent that could be to use stronger priors on the spatial field to limit its flexibility. I thus tried using smaller sd for the field while keeping the range constant. This didn't seem to change the situation much unless I used very small sd or fixed it to some small value.

To better understand what was going on, I studied the relation between the posterior mean sigma and the prior for sigma and this is what I found (see image below). All other priors were kept at the same values. The range was set to prior.range = c(5, 0.01) (a 1% chance the range if inferior to 5km) and sigma was set to prior.sigma  = c(sigma, 0.01) ( a 1% chance sd is superior to sigma).

There is a sharp change in the posterior mean sigma at around sigma = 0.04 and on each side of this change, the posterior mean sigma are quite similar. Importantly, for any reasonable sigma value I would use, the posterior mean sigma is roughly the same (~ 1.3). In this case, I expect that my fixed effects should explain only a small fraction of the counts and that the variance of the spatial field should be quite large. Hence, anything below c(1, 0.01) would appear highly unreasonable (even on the scale of the linear predictor) and thus all reasonable sigma seem to lead to almost the same posterior sigma.

Is this expected behaviour for a pc prior on the sd of a spatial field? Are pc prior more prone to threshold effects compared to standard priors? Perhaps the impact of pc priors is more related to what the data says compared to what the modeler thinks? Or could this indicate some problem with the model?

Thanks in advance for the input
François Rousseu

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] unexpected intra-variant variances estimation in disaggregation spatial regression model using INLA()
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

there isn't enough information provided to know for sure. If the nugget variance from the 100x100 grid is sigma^2, then the nugget variance on the 10x10averaged grid is sigma^2 / 100 (average of 100 independent iid variables).
So in a perfect world your nugget variance estimate should be 1/100 times the fine resolution nugget variance.
In practice, it will likely differ from that due to interaction with the numerical representation of the random field itself, and due to non-identifiability of the covariance parameters (with only a single field realisation, the parameters are not fully identifiable).

Finn

messages.subject: Slow model fitting with a Type III spatiotemporal interaction
messages.subject_clean: Slow model fitting with a Type III spatiotemporal interaction
messages.body_plain:
Dear R-INLA community:

Hello, I am working on models with spatiotemporal interaction terms.

I found that fitting models with a type-III (unstructured temporal * structured spatial) model took a much longer time than fitting models with the other three types of spatiotemporal interaction terms. I guessed this is because the rank is a bit higher ((n-1)T; following Blangiardo and Cameletti 2015:241) than that of other counterparts, but this does not hold as the type-I interaction has the higher rank (nT).

I think this is counterintuitive as well as against the assumption suggested in Vincente et al. (2020:1429; https://doi.org/10.1007/s00477-020-01808-x), quote:

"Regarding computing times for the models presented in Sect. 2, models with Type II and Type IV interactions are the slowest regardless of the fitting technique ... One reason for this may be that the number of constraints is much higher for Type II and Type IV than for the Type I and Type III counterparts."

If I understood correctly, the matrix for Type-III would be more sparse than that of Type-IV, because Type-III takes a diagonal matrix for the temporal term. A reproducible example taken from Chapter 7.1.2 in Blangiardo and Cameletti (2015) (attached) yielded running time in my laptop as below (*please note that no 'experimental' feature in the up-to-date version of INLA package was applied here):

Type I: 10.1 seconds
Type II: 53.1 seconds
Type III: 327 seconds
Type IV: 63.6 seconds

I am suffering from this issue right now since I aim to compare four types of spatiotemporal interactions with much larger data. The model with Type III interaction term with my data (3108*14) fits terribly slow and consumes 60+GB of memory from time to time (even with PARDISO and experimental feature of the testing version of INLA). I hope I can understand why Type III interaction takes a longer time than other interactions from your insight.

Thank you very much.

Best,

messages.subject: Include an interaction term with time in the Cox PH model
messages.subject_clean: Include an interaction term with time in the Cox PH model
messages.body_plain:
Hello R-inla users,

I am interested in fitting a Cox PH model where there is an interaction term with time. There are two approaches I can use:
1) I can include the interaction term directly in the model
2) use the counting process approach to expand my dataset and then fit the model.

I tried both, but my results don't match with the leukemia dataset in BUGS.

Here is my work for approach 1)

sinla.vet <- inla.surv(data_sim$obs.t, data_sim$fail)
coxinla.vet <- inla(sinla.vet ~  Z + Z*log(obs.t), data = data_sim,
                    family = "coxph")

Here is my work for approach 2) using the counting process:

#Expand dataset using counting process and survSplit, cut points are unique event times
#Each subject will have observations at all unique time points, until they have an event and are removed from the risk set.

data_sim2 <- survSplit(Surv(data_sim$obs.t, data_sim$fail) ~., data_sim, cut=c(1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,10,11,12,13,15,16,17,22,23,35))

#Use interval censoring approach where there is a start time and stop time
sinla.vet <- inla.surv(data_sim2$tstart, data_sim2$event, data_sim2$tstop)
coxinla.vet <- inla(sinla.vet ~  Z +  Z*log(tstop), data = data_sim2,
                    family = "coxph")

Thank you. I appreciate any help with this.

messages.subject: Re: Slow model fitting with a Type III spatiotemporal interaction
messages.subject_clean: Slow model fitting with a Type III spatiotemporal interaction
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

It should not be the case: type 3 is slower than type 4. The speed depends on the number of constraints each type has.  The precision matrix is composed of at least 5 blocks: RW (size n) (of order L and L usually equals to 1 or 2), iid (size n, time), besag (size m), iid (size m, space) and rgeneric (type 1,2,3 or 4: which is the Kronecker product of two of the previous models).

The number of constraints in each type:
1. type 1: L + 1
2. type 2: Lm + L + 1
3. type 3: n + L + 1
4. type 4: Lm + n - 1

Make sure you use the right model for the interaction model using "generic0", and the right rank for the matrix.

 f(id,
    model="generic0",
    Cmatrix = ,
    constr= ,
    extraconstr = ,
    rankdef= )

You need to use "extraconstr" to list the constraints you have in each case, which I didn't see in the code. You can use eigen decomposition to find these constraints. "constr" does only sum to zero constraint. However, it can be implemented in different ways, but this is what do I recommend.

Best Regards,
Esmail

> Dear R-INLA community:
>
> Hello, I am working on models with spatiotemporal interaction terms.
>
> I found that fitting models with a type-III (unstructured temporal * structured spatial) model took a much longer time than fitting models with the other three types of spatiotemporal interaction terms. I guessed this is because the rank is a bit higher ((n-1)T; following Blangiardo and Cameletti 2015:241) than that of other counterparts, but this does not hold as the type-I interaction has the higher rank (nT).
>
> I think this is counterintuitive as well as against the assumption suggested in Vincente et al. (2020:1429; https://doi.org/10.1007/s00477-020-01808-x), quote:
>
> "Regarding computing times for the models presented in Sect. 2, models with Type II and Type IV interactions are the slowest regardless of the fitting technique ... One reason for this may be that the number of constraints is much higher for Type II and Type IV than for the Type I and Type III counterparts."
>
> If I understood correctly, the matrix for Type-III would be more sparse than that of Type-IV, because Type-III takes a diagonal matrix for the temporal term. A reproducible example taken from Chapter 7.1.2 in Blangiardo and Cameletti (2015) (attached) yielded running time in my laptop as below (*please note that no 'experimental' feature in the up-to-date version of INLA package was applied here):
>
> Type I: 10.1 seconds
> Type II: 53.1 seconds
> Type III: 327 seconds
> Type IV: 63.6 seconds
>
> I am suffering from this issue right now since I aim to compare four types of spatiotemporal interactions with much larger data. The model with Type III interaction term with my data (3108*14) fits terribly slow and consumes 60+GB of memory from time to time (even with PARDISO and experimental feature of the testing version of INLA). I hope I can understand why Type III interaction takes a longer time than other interactions from your insight.
>
> Thank you very much.
>
> Best,

messages.subject: Comparing the spatial effects of two models
messages.subject_clean: Comparing the spatial effects of two models
messages.body_plain:
hello,

I have a question about comparing the spatial effects of two models using r-inla. Assuming I have two models: Model 1 and Model 2. Where Model  1 is a survival model with the formula (adopted from Martine, Akerkar & Rue (2011):

f1 = inla.surv(time, event)∼ PM+ f(ID, model="iid", param=c(1, 1))

and Model 2 is expressed as

f1 = inla.surv(time, event)∼ PM+ age + edu + inc + f(ID, model="iid", param=c(1, 1))

where ID is an index for spatial units.

Is there a way to compare the spatial effects from the two models in terms of change in the spatial risk? Can I just do such a comparison by looking at the differences in the log hazards for ID in the two models (e.g. Model 1 - Model 2)?

Thank you.

messages.body_plain:
Maybe you want to compare DIC or WAIC, if you're up to a model
comparison. Otherwise, if you're after the chance in the risk, you have
to check how to risk for the two fits differ.

On Fri, 2021-12-03 at 05:25 -0800, Prince Michael Amegbor wrote:
> hello,
>
> I have a question about comparing the spatial effects of two models
> using r-inla. Assuming I have two models: Model 1 and Model 2. Where
> Model  1 is a survival model with the formula (adopted from Martine,
> Akerkar & Rue (2011):
>
> f1 = inla.surv(time, event)∼ PM+ f(ID, model="iid", param=c(1, 1))
>
> and Model 2 is expressed as
>
> f1 = inla.surv(time, event)∼ PM+ age + edu + inc + f(ID, model="iid",
> param=c(1, 1))
>
> where ID is an index for spatial units.
>
> Is there a way to compare the spatial effects from the two models in
> terms of change in the spatial risk? Can I just do such a comparison
> by looking at the differences in the log hazards for ID in the two
> models (e.g. Model 1 - Model 2)?
>
> Thank you.
>
>

messages.body_plain:
I think this is a case where you're using R-4.0 and the package is
compiled for R-4.1.  If that is the case, please upgrade to R-4.1

On Sat, 2021-12-04 at 02:20 -0800, Barry Thierno Souleymane wrote:
> Hello,
>
> I am fitting a MCAR model for two binary outcomes from my data. The
> model run  but INLA crashes when fitting the MCAR model on the data.
> There is window that appears and the message is "Fatal error: unable
> to initialize the JIT"
>
> Error in inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed() :
>   The inla-program exited with an error. Unless you interupted it
> yourself, please rerun with verbose=TRUE and check the output
> carefully.
>   If this does not help, please contact the developers at
> <he...@r-inla.org>.
>
> Please,  anyone experienced in such kind of issue? How can I solve
> it?
>
> There are below  the codes I have used:
>
> library(sf)
> library(sp)
> library(maptools)
> # loads sp library
> library(maps)
>
> # read in shape files (single folder with all associated files, no
>
> x<-st_read("C:\\Users\\Alexis
> H\\Downloads\\gin_admbnda_ocha_fis\\gin_admbnda_adm1_ocha.shp")
> str(x)
> # display the shapefile
> plot(x)
> str(x)
> library("spdep")
>
> #Compute sparse adjacency matrix
>
> Guineaadj <- poly2nb(x, queen = FALSE)
>
> Guinea.adj <-nb2mat(Guineaadj, style = "B")
>
> Guinea.adj <- as(Guinea.adj, "dgTMatrix")
>
> # joint model
> #devtools::install_github("becarioprecario/INLAMSM")
> install.packages('INLAMSM')
> library(INLA)
> library(INLAMSM)
> require(spdep)
> require(spData)
> require(rgdal)
>
> # Proper MCAR model
> #Data
>
>
> dta <- data.frame(Y12 =c(Final_data$Outcome, Final_data$Outcome2),
> E=c(Final_data$Age, Final_data$Age),
>                    E=c(Final_data$Gender, Final_data$Gender))
>
> dta$Var1 <-
> c(rep(1,length(Final_data$Outcome)),rep(2,length(Final_data$Outcome)))
>
> k=2 #number of diseases
>
> # Range of autocorrelation parameter
>
> alpha.min <- 0 #Minimum value of the spatial autocorrelation
> parameter.
> alpha.max <- 1 #Maximum value of the spatial autocorrelation
> parameter.
>
> #Define MCAR model
>
> model.mcar <- inla.MCAR.model(k = k, W = Guinea.adj, alpha.min =
> alpha.min,alpha.max = alpha.max)
>
> MCAR <- inla(Y12 ~ 0+f(Var1, model = model.mcar), data = dta,
>               control.compute = list(waic=T,cpo = T, dic = T), #
> compute DIC, CPO
>               family ="binomial",
>               Ntrials = 1, #marginal distribution for the outcome,
> expected count,
>               control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),verbose=TRUE)
>
> #total model summary
> summary(MCAR)
>

messages.body_plain:
Thank you,
Below are R codes and attached the zipped folder in which we have the shapefile named "gin_admbnda_adm1_ocha.shp"

# dependent variable 1
rm(list=ls())
memory.limit()
memory.limit(size= 1000000)

prop <- c(0.3,0.5,0.6,0.7,0.8,0.3,0.3,0.2)
for(i in 1:8)
{
  data  <- replicate(200,{
    sample<- rbinom(8,1,prop[i]) })

}

# dependent variable 2
prop <- c(0.4,0.5,0.6,0.5,0.7,0.5,0.3,0.6)
for(i in 1:8)
{
  data2  <- replicate(200,{
    sample<- rbinom(8,1,prop[i]) })

}

library(INLA)

# independent variables

mu <- c(43,40,46,50,53,54,46,49)
std <- c(2.3,2.4,2.1,2.5,2.7,2.9,2.0,2.1)

for(i in 1:8)
{
  age <- replicate(200,
                   {
                     samplew <- round(rnorm(8,mu[i],std[i]),0)
                   })
}

# gender

gender  <- replicate(200,{
  sample<- rbinom(8,1,0.5) })

library(reshape2)

# cleaned format

Age_child <- melt(age, value.name <http://value.name> = "Age")

Y <- melt(data,value.name <http://value.name> = "Outcome" )

Gender_child <- melt(gender, value.name <http://value.name> = "Gender")

Y2 <- melt(data2,value.name <http://value.name> = "Outcome2" )

# joining

library(dplyr)

Merged_data <- inner_join(Y,Age_child, by = c("Var1","Var2"))

Merged_data1 <- inner_join(Merged_data, Gender_child,by = c("Var1","Var2"))
Merged_data2 <- inner_join(Merged_data1, Y2, by = c("Var1","Var2"))

# variables of interest

Final_data <- select(Merged_data2, Outcome,Outcome2, Age, Var1, Gender)
head(Final_data)

library(sf)
library(sp)
library(maptools)
# loads sp library
library(maps)

# read in shape files

x<-st_read("...................................\\gin_admbnda_ocha_fis\\gin_admbnda_adm1_ocha.shp")

library("spdep")

#Compute sparse adjacency matrix

Guineaadj <- poly2nb(x, queen = FALSE)

Guinea.adj <-nb2mat(Guineaadj, style = "B")

Guinea.adj <- as(Guinea.adj, "dgTMatrix")

# joint model
#devtools::install_github("becarioprecario/INLAMSM")

##install.packages('INLAMSM')
library(INLA)
library(INLAMSM)

# Proper MCAR model

#Data

dta <- data.frame(Y12 =c(Final_data$Outcome, Final_data$Outcome2), E=c(Final_data$Age, Final_data$ Gender ))

dta$Var1 <- c(rep(1,length(Final_data$Outcome)),rep(2,length(Final_data$Outcome)))

k=2 #number of diseases

# Range of autocorrelation parameter

alpha.min <- 0 #Minimum value of the spatial autocorrelation parameter.
alpha.max <- 1 #Maximum value of the spatial autocorrelation parameter.

#Define MCAR model

model.mcar <- inla.MCAR.model(k = k, W = Guinea.adj, alpha.min = alpha.min,alpha.max = alpha.max)

MCAR <- inla(Y12 ~ E+f(Var1, model = model.mcar), data = dta,

              control.compute = list(waic=T,cpo = T, dic = T), # compute DIC, CPO
               family ="binomial",
              Ntrials = 1, #marginal distribution for the outcome, expected count,
              control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),verbose=TRUE)

#total model summary
summary(MCAR)

Hi  Håvard,

Thanks so much! This helped a lot. I found the "experimental" mode to work much better for running the models, and it was much faster too.

- Kristin

On Tuesday, November 16, 2021 at 3:04:09 AM UTC-5 he...@r-inla.org wrote:
> On Mon, 2021-11-15 at 15:27 -0800, KB wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > I am running several R-INLA SPDE models with different covariates and
> > using DIC to select the best model. When I run some of the models, I
> > obtain a Hessian warning being less than 0, which has consequence for
> > the accuracy of the hyperparameter.
> >
> > I am able to correct the Hessian warning either by lowering the
> > tolerance to 1e-10 or by rerunning using result = inla.rerun().
>
> rerun would likely fix this easier. If you run with R-4.1 a newer/st
> testing version, then there is a built-in rerun as well.
>
> you may try to add
>
> inla(..., inla.mode="experimental")
>
> which should also help (additional to being faster)
>
> >
> > 2) To compare models using DIC, do I run all of the models (regardless
> > of whether they obtain Hessian warnings) using inla.rerun or with a
> > lower tolerance, or do I just do these adjustments on the models that
> > produce Hessian warnings?
>
> I would guess DIC would be less affected by this, but generally you want
> to get the Hessian right.
>
> you may check automatically for this with
>
> r <- inla(...)
> if (sum(abs(r$misc$cov.intern[upper.tri(r$misc$cov.intern)])) == 0) {
> r <- inla.rerun(r)
> }
>
>
> --
> Håvard Rue
> he...@r-inla.org

messages.subject: Can I and how do I specify a heteroscedastic Gaussian noise in a spatial SPDE model ?
messages.subject_clean: Can I and how do I specify a heteroscedastic Gaussian noise in a spatial SPDE model ?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm new to INLA so I might be asking silly questions.
I am working with a SPDE model for Gaussian data with spatial auto-correlation, with the classical formmulation

y(u) = X(u)Beta + w(u) + epsilon(u),
u being the coordinate of the spatial observations.
X() being covariates.
Beta being a vector of regression coefficients.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

There are other approaches (such as inla.rgeneric), but one way is to take advantage of the internal spde model implementation, that allows you to use other matrices than those from the SPDE construction; in the inla.spde.generic function, M0, M1, and M2 would usually be c0, g1, and g2 (with some scaling factors) from inla.mesh.fem(), but you could set M0=I and M1=M2=0 to be able to build your epsilon(u) model via the tau parameter (and make kappa fixed to 1).

For the model with loglinear variance w.r.t. a covariate matrix X (note: just as for the spde models, keep the dimension ncol(X) small!)
  epsilon = N(0, diag(2 * X * beta))
the precision matrix is
  Q = T %*% M0 %*% T
where T is diagonal with logarithm X %*% beta and M0 is an identity matrix

the code should look like this (or similar; I haven't tested all the matrix details):

model <-
  inla.spde2.generic(M0 = Diagonal(n=nrow(X), x=1.0), M1 = Diagonal(n=nrow(X), x=0.0), M2 = Diagonal(n=nrow(X), x=0.0),
    B0 = cbind(0, X), B1 = matrix(0, 1, 1+ ncol(X)), B2 = matrix(0, 1, 1+ ncol(X)),
    theta.mu <http://theta.mu> = rep(0,ncol(X)),
    theta.Q = diag(rep(1,ncol(X))),
    transform = "identity")

the beta priors above are all set to N(0,1) via theta.mu <http://theta.mu> and theta.Q; change them to something more reasonable for your problem.

You then use it just like the spde models, but with the A matrix set to Diagonal(1.0, n)

Finn

the memory estimate

it also depends on the number of threads used, as the required memory
for a fixed model its like

	A + B * num.threads

for some A and B.

library(INLA)
inla.setOption(inla.mode="experimental")

as this should use less memory

messages.body_plain:

Le lundi 6 décembre 2021 à 18:08:52 UTC+1, finn.l...@gmail.com a écrit :
> Hi,
>
> There are other approaches (such as inla.rgeneric), but one way is to take advantage of the internal spde model implementation, that allows you to use other matrices than those from the SPDE construction; in the inla.spde.generic function, M0, M1, and M2 would usually be c0, g1, and g2 (with some scaling factors) from inla.mesh.fem(), but you could set M0=I and M1=M2=0 to be able to build your epsilon(u) model via the tau parameter (and make kappa fixed to 1).
>
> For the model with loglinear variance w.r.t. a covariate matrix X (note: just as for the spde models, keep the dimension ncol(X) small!)
>   epsilon = N(0, diag(2 * X * beta))
> the precision matrix is
>   Q = T %*% M0 %*% T
> where T is diagonal with logarithm X %*% beta and M0 is an identity matrix
>
> the code should look like this (or similar; I haven't tested all the matrix details):
>
> model <-
>   inla.spde2.generic(M0 = Diagonal(n=nrow(X), x=1.0), M1 = Diagonal(n=nrow(X), x=0.0), M2 = Diagonal(n=nrow(X), x=0.0),
>     B0 = cbind(0, X), B1 = matrix(0, 1, 1+ ncol(X)), B2 = matrix(0, 1, 1+ ncol(X)),
>     theta.mu <http://theta.mu> = rep(0,ncol(X)),
>     theta.Q = diag(rep(1,ncol(X))),
>     transform = "identity")
>
> the beta priors above are all set to N(0,1) via theta.mu <http://theta.mu> and theta.Q; change them to something more reasonable for your problem.
>
> You then use it just like the spde models, but with the A matrix set to Diagonal(1.0, n)
>
> Finn
>
> On Mon, 6 Dec 2021 at 16:43, Sébastien Coube <sebasti...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi all,
> >
> > I'm new to INLA so I might be asking silly questions.
> > I am working with a SPDE model for Gaussian data with spatial auto-correlation, with the classical formmulation
> >
> > y(u) = X(u)Beta + w(u) + epsilon(u),
> > u being the coordinate of the spatial observations.
> > X() being covariates.
> > Beta being a vector of regression coefficients.
> > w() accounting for spatial auto-correlation and being a Gaussian (Markov) random field.
> > epsilon() accounting for independent errors.
> > Thanks to several references such as https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/spde-gitbook/ch-nonstationarity.html   or https://sites.google.com/a/r-inla.org/stbook/, I could figure out how to specify varying range and marginal variance for w() through the Btau and Bkappa matrices. However, I also would like to integrate covariates to explain the log-variance of epsilon() so that the resulting noise is heteroscedastic. Could someone give me a hint ?
> >
> > Thank you in advance

messages.subject: question about syntax when having different random walks for two groups in stack
messages.subject_clean: question about syntax when having different random walks for two groups in stack
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am trying to create a random walk for two different groups of observations in a single model. When not using a stack, this can be achieved in INLA using e.g.

inla(y ~  f(time1, is1,model="rw1") + f(time2, is2,model="rw1"),
               data=testdata,
               family="gaussian",
               control.predictor=list( compute=TRUE),
               verbose=TRUE)
where is1 is a vector of 0,1 indicating group membership. Likewise for is2. When I try to apply the same approach using a stack I get an error (see my example code below, data generation is based on documentation for inla.stack()). I am hoping that somebody can point me in the right direction.

Thanks in advance,

Jan Jaap

n = 200
loc = matrix(runif(n*2),n,2)
mesh      = inla.mesh.create.helper(points.domain=loc, max.edge=c(0.05, 0.2))
proj.obs  = inla.mesh.projector(mesh, loc=loc)
spde = inla.spde2.matern(mesh,
                         B.tau=cbind(log(1), 1, 0),
                         B.kappa=matrix(c(log(sqrt(8)/0.2), 0, 1), 1, 3))

time1 <- time2 <-  1:n
is1 <- rep(0:1, length.out=200)
is2 <- 1-is1

field = inla.qsample(n=1, Q=inla.spde2.precision(spde, theta=c(0,0)))[,1]
y = 2*time1 + inla.mesh.project(proj.obs, field)

#########################################################
#working example without use of stack
##########################################################

testdata <- data.frame("time1"=time1, "time2"=time2, "is1"=is1, "is2"=is2)
result2 = inla(y ~  f(time1, is1,model="rw1") + f(time2, is2,model="rw1"),
               data=testdata,
               family="gaussian",
               control.predictor=list( compute=TRUE),
               verbose=TRUE)

#############################################################
#Now with stack (Fails because "variable lengths differ (found for 'is1')")
##############################################################

mystack <-  inla.stack(data    = list(y=y),
                     A       = list(1,1,1),
                     effects = list(intercept=rep(1, length(y)),
                                    time1=time1,
                                    time2=time2
                     )
)

formula = y ~ -1 + intercept + f(time1, is1, model="rw1") + f(time2, is2, model="rw1")

result2 = inla(formula,
               data=inla.stack.data(mystack),
               family="gaussian",
               control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(mystack), compute=TRUE),
               verbose=TRUE)

Hi,

For this, I see two options to fix it:
Either add is1 and is2 to the effects lists, with list(list(intercept=…),list(time1,is1),list(time2,is2))
(I haven’t checked if the resulting NA entries in the is-vectors where time1/2 will also be NA will cause a problem or not)
Or remove the weights arguments from the f() specifications and instead use
A=list(1,Diagonal(length(is1),is1),Diagonal(length(is2),is2)),
Which has the same effect as weights in f().

Finn

Hi Finn,

Thanks for the swift response. Much appreciated. Both your suggested approaches worked, and yield the same result. However, the results are different from when the syntax without stack was used. Whereas the intercept means are the same for all models, the intercept sd and the precisions for the Gaussian observations and the two random walks differ when using the stack versus when using the original call. The code below demonstrates this.

Am I still doing something wrong or misunderstanding the results?

Jan Jaap

n = 200
loc = matrix(runif(n*2),n,2)
mesh      = inla.mesh.create.helper(points.domain=loc, max.edge=c(0.05, 0.2))
proj.obs  = inla.mesh.projector(mesh, loc=loc)
spde = inla.spde2.matern(mesh,
                         B.tau=cbind(log(1), 1, 0),
                         B.kappa=matrix(c(log(sqrt(8)/0.2), 0, 1), 1, 3))

time1 <- time2 <-  1:n
is1 <- rep(0:1, length.out=200)
is2 <- 1-is1

field = inla.qsample(n=1, Q=inla.spde2.precision(spde, theta=c(0,0)))[,1]
y = 2*time1 + inla.mesh.project(proj.obs, field)

#########################################################

#without W, two  time series

##########################################################

testdata <- data.frame("time1"=time1, "time2"=time2, "is1"=is1, "is2"=is2)

result1 = inla(y ~  f(time1, is1,model="rw1") + f(time2, is2,model="rw1"),

               data=testdata,
               family="gaussian",
               control.predictor=list( compute=TRUE),
               verbose=TRUE)

#############################################################

#Now with stack, using diagonals in observation matrices

##############################################################

mystack <-  inla.stack(data    = list(y=y),

                     A       = list(1,Diagonal(length(is1),is1),Diagonal(length(is2),is2)),

                     effects = list(intercept=rep(1, length(y)),
                                    time1=time1,
                                    time2=time2)
)

formula = y ~ -1 + intercept + f(time1,  model="rw1") + f(time2,  model="rw1")

result2 = inla(formula,
               data=inla.stack.data(mystack),
               family="gaussian",
               control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(mystack), compute=TRUE),
               verbose=TRUE)

#############################################################
#Now with stack, adding is1 and is2 to the effects list

##############################################################

mystack <-  inla.stack(data    = list(y=y),

                       A       = list(1,Diagonal(length(is1),is1),Diagonal(length(is2),is2)),
                       effects = list(list(intercept=rep(1, length(y))),
                                      list(time1=time1, is1= is1),
                                      list(time2=time2, is2= is2))

                       )

formula = y ~ -1 + intercept + f(time1, is1,  model="rw1") + f(time2, is2,  model="rw1")

result3 = inla(formula,

               data=inla.stack.data(mystack),
               family="gaussian",
               control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(mystack), compute=TRUE),
               verbose=TRUE)

summary(result1) #syntax without stack
summary(result2) #stack, using observation matrices
summary(result3) #stack, adding is1 and is2 to effects list

You didn’t include the actual results, but if you try the non-stack version but with an explicit intercept as a covariate (set intercept=1 in your data object) I suspect the results will be the same. The auto-intercept has a smaller precision(zero, I believe) than other fixed effects, so the models aren’t identical.
You can set the prior for a fixed effect e.g. with
  f(intercept,model=“linear”, prec.linear=…)
(Check the INLA::f documentation)

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Can I and how do I specify a heteroscedastic Gaussian noise in a spatial SPDE model ?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Can I and how do I specify a heteroscedastic Gaussian noise in a spatial SPDE model ?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Finn,

I went on with my implementation but a few points are confusing me.

The first point is that I have about 50000 spatial observations, and using the standard mesh constructors of INLA I have a mesh with about 20000 nodes.
I understood that the B_kappa and B_tau matrices of the coherent spatial effect w(u) must have 20000 rows : each row of B_kappa, B_tau corresponds to the value of the covariates taken at the mesh nodes. Just to be sure, do the X you mentioned in your answer correspond to covariates evaluated at the mesh nodes or at the observations ? In other words, in my case, is the n you mentioned equal to 20000 or to 50000 ?

The second point is how I should combine the spatially coherent spatial effect and the heteroscedastic noise in the same model. I started from simple examples I saw in the tutorials and tinkered a solution using INLA::inla.stack() . While I have no bug when I run that (it's something !), I still have doubts about the validity of this code. Does my stack and formula construction seem sound to you ?

stk <- INLA::inla.stack(
  data = list(y = observed_field),
  A = list(A_noise,    # the Identity matrix you mentioned
                A_field,     # generated using the mesh and INLA::inla.spde.make.A()
                1               # for fixed effects
                ),
  effects=list(
    INLA::inla.spde.make.index(name = "heteroscedastic.noise", spde_noise$n.spde                        ),  #the noise index
    INLA::inla.spde.make.index(name = "spatial.field",                    spde_spatially_coherent$n.spde ),  #the spatial field index
    X_split                                                                                                                                                               #a list containing the covariates for fixed effects
  ))

formula = observed_field ~
  - 1 +                                                                                            # removing superfluous intercept as advised by INLA
  dairp + dmino + dquksig + dTRI + gcarb + globedem +    # fixed effects
  nlights03 + sdroads + twi + vsky + winde +                        # fixed effects
  f(heteroscedastic.noise, model = spde_noise)+                # heteroskedastic Gaussian noise
  f(spatial.field, model = spde_spatially_coherent)              # spatially coherent random effect

Last question, about the link function family. While I assume my data to be Gaussian, it feels redundant to fill the argument family="gaussian" in the INLA::inla() function. Indeed, the Gaussian noise is be captured by the SPDE you gave me, and once the fixed effects, the spatially coherent field, and the heteroscedastic noise are added, there is nothing left.
Therefore, it feels much more natural to me to use the control.family argument like https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/spde-gitbook/ch-nonstationarity.html . In their toy example, they have a noise-less data set, so they force the latent field to stick to the observed data. This is exactly what I want to do, except that I have two latent fields.
This gives me the following code, again does it look sound to you ?

clik <- list(hyper = list(prec = list(initial = 20,  fixed = TRUE))) very high precision of Gaussian observations
res <- INLA::inla(
            formula,                                                                                                                    # the aformentioned formula
            data = INLA::inla.stack.data(stk),                                                                         # the aformentioned stack
            control.family = clik,                                                                                                # control family with high precision
            control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, A = INLA::inla.stack.A(stk)),
            verbose = T)

Once again, many many thanks for your answer !
Sébastien

messages.body_plain:
Using the "zero observations" approach will in theory give the same result as Dirichlet conditions; A dirichlet condition it precisely that; an imposed zero value at/outside the boundary.

The "remove rows/columns" approach achieves the same thing by noting that in the basis function representation
u(s) =  \sum_{j=1}^N \psi_j(s) w_j,

setting u(s)=0 on the boundary is the same thing as setting all w_j=0 for nodes on the boundary, which in turn is the same thing as not including those basis functions in the sum.
For the precision, the argument is similar; the precision for the interior node weights is the submatrix of the precision belonging to the interior nodes.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Can I and how do I specify a heteroscedastic Gaussian noise in a spatial SPDE model ?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Can I and how do I specify a heteroscedastic Gaussian noise in a spatial SPDE model ?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The heteroscedastic noise component is unrelated to the mesh, since it contributes directly to each individual observations, so the number of rows should equal the number of observations, i.e. 50000.

One thing to keep in mind is that when you construct the mesh, you don't have to use the observation points as "seed points"; in fact, doing that can cause problematic node clusters when there is a lot of locations. Instead, focus on the resolution of the mesh, so that it can capture the needed spatial scales (At least in the vicinity of data).  A practical way to do that is to increase the cutoff value, which will make it ignore many of the input points, and produce a smoother triangulation, usually with fewer triangles.

A follow-up email about the need for the control.family trick get stuck in my drafts; yes, setting the observation precision to a large value is the right way here.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: How does the INLA model handle 0 values in continuous variables?
messages.subject_clean: How does the INLA model handle 0 values in continuous variables?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Wen,

For zero-inflated continuous distributions, an additional option that you can fit with R-INLA is the two-part model. It consists in a decomposition of the distribution of your zero-inflated continuous outcome into a binary outcome (probability of zero) and a positive continuous outcome (where you can specify a lognormal or gamma likelihood). It corresponds to the hurdle model for zero-inflated count data. We made a paper where we fit this model to a longitudinal zero-inflated continuous outcome jointly with survival times, see https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.13704.pdf

And you can take a look at the associated R code available here: https://github.com/DenisRustand/TPJM_sim/blob/master/TPJM_INLA.R

Best,
Denis Rustand
he...@r-inla.org

messages.subject: Years-specific SRF
messages.subject_clean: Years-specific SRF
messages.body_plain:
Hi

We fitted a NegBinomial INLA model to our data on fish catches. Adding a SRF (Spatial Random Field) decreased DIC substantially. See code below.
However, we know that the fish are located differently from year to year, so we want to make the SRF year-speciffic instead. The spatial correlation distance should be the same from year to year

How can we implement in the code below?

Any advice would be highly appreciated
Søren and Teunis

#* Section 8.3: Stack---- Define the stack for model M2
Stack2 <- inla.stack(
  tag = "Fit2",
  data = list(FishCount = dfModelData$FishCount ),
  A = list(1, 1, 1, A2),
  effects = list(
    Intercept = rep(1, N),  #Intercept
    X = Xm[,-1],            #Covariates without the intercept
    XDepth_m = XDepth_m,    #Smoother f(Primary
    w = w2.index))          #SRF

#* Section 8.4: Formula for the spatial NegBin GAM----
f2 <- formula(FishCount ~ -1 + Intercept +
                fYear2004 + fYear2005 + fYear2006  + #Year effects
                Xkm.std + Ykm.std + #UTM coordinates
               OtherCovariateA + OtherCovariateB + #Other linear covariates
                XDepth_m + #Smoother on depth
                f(w, model = spde2))

#* Section 8.5: Execute the spatial NegBin GAM----
M2 <- inla(f2,
           lincomb = lcs.Depth_m,
           family = "nbinomial",
           data = inla.stack.data(Stack2),
           control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE),
           control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(Stack2)))

then

or
	f(idx, model="iid", replicate=one)

is the same as

	f(one, model="iid", replicate=idx)

messages.subject: Correct steps to improve INLA speed and performances when using random effects
messages.subject_clean: Correct steps to improve INLA speed and performances when using random effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I would like to open this post since I am quite sure I am running my INLA model with wrong settings when using random effects. I am modelling counts at the pixel level in a subcontinental region (north of Europe) and the spatial resolution is approximately 10x10 km2, hence I have almost 30,000 observations. My INLA model configuration is the following:

inla.setOption(pardiso.license = "~/PATH_TO_PARDISO_LICENCE/pardiso.lic")

inla(formula = outcome ~ 1 + f(ID, model = "iid") + f(ID2, model = "matern2d", nu = 1,
                                                                                            nrow = rows, ncol = cols),
        family = "poisson",
        data = grid@data,
         control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE,
                                                  link = 1),
         control.compute = list(config = TRUE,
                                                  openmp.strategy = "pardiso"),
                                                  dic = TRUE,
                                                  waic = TRUE,
                                                  cpo = TRUE),
         control.inla(strategy = "simplified.laplace",
                               huge = TRUE),
         E = cellarea,
         num.threads = 8,
         verbose = FALSE))

I've highlighted the Matérn model because that's the part that slows down everything. Without it the model runs in almost 2 minutes. When I run this model on my iMac with 8 cores (32 Gb per core) AND the pardiso licence it takes way more than four hours. However, when I put everything on the cluster (without pardiso) and I increase the cores and memory (30 x 20Gb) it takes more or less one hour.

I've read some posts in the group and I noticed that people run models with the same number of observations without so much problems, so I would like to understand what I am doing wrong. In particular:
should I change parameters inside the control.inla function?
is there a way to modify the Matérn random effect in order to make it run faster, for example by specifying the hyperparameters? And, if yes, how?
Thank you so much in advance for your help, and I hope this post might help also others facing this issue.

Nico

在2021年12月8日星期三 UTC+1 19:58:19<Denis Rustand> 写道：
> Hi Wen,
>
> For zero-inflated continuous distributions, an additional option that you can fit with R-INLA is the two-part model. It consists in a decomposition of the distribution of your zero-inflated continuous outcome into a binary outcome (probability of zero) and a positive continuous outcome (where you can specify a lognormal or gamma likelihood). It corresponds to the hurdle model for zero-inflated count data. We made a paper where we fit this model to a longitudinal zero-inflated continuous outcome jointly with survival times, see https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.13704.pdf
>
> And you can take a look at the associated R code available here: https://github.com/DenisRustand/TPJM_sim/blob/master/TPJM_INLA.R
>
> Best,
> Denis Rustand

messages.subject: Question about validation
messages.subject_clean: Question about validation
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have a question regarding code for validating models using R-INLA-SPDE that I was hoping someone might be able to offer some advice. I am trying to validate a negative binomial model by comparing the predictions vs. the observed results of a subset of the data that was held out of the full dataset to be used for validation.

I found the predicted vs. observed values of the validation dataset to be quite different. I was wondering if there is something wrong with the code I am using or if there is another method of validation that I could use? I read about sampling from the posterior distribution, but was not sure of how to interpret the output once I sampled from it and am unsure if it would produce  different results from what I have used with the method below.

The code and output are below.

Sincerely,

Kristin

The summary of predicted values and observed values from the code below are as follows: The correlation between the observed and predicted values was 0.40.

#Output from predictions made from validation dataset

     Min.         1st Qu.        Median      Mean           3rd Qu.          Max.

  0.079              3.89         10.54           17.02          22.62          237.45

#Output of observed values

   Min.            1st Qu.        Median     Mean             3rd Qu.           Max.

   0.00               0.00              3.00         18.56            13.00           2246.00

The code I have used is below:

Loc <- cbind(train$x, train$y)

Loc1 <- cbind(validation$x, validation$y)

ConvHull <- inla.nonconvex.hull(Loc, convex = 15000, concave = 20000)

Mesh3 <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary = ConvHull, max.edge = c(15000, 75000), cutoff = (3000), offset = c(15000, 75000))

A_est <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = Mesh3, loc = Loc)

A.pred <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = Mesh3, loc = Loc1)

spde1 <- inla.spde2.matern(Mesh3, alpha = 2)

spde1$n.spde

s.index <- inla.spde.make.index(name = "spatial.field2", n.spde = spde1$n.spde)

dep.stack <- inla.stack(data  = list(Y = train$Y),

                        A = list(A_est, 1),

                        effects = list(c(s.index, list(Intercept=1)),

                                       list(A = train$A,

                                             B = train$B,

                                            C = train$C,

                                            D = train$D,

                                            E = train$E)),

                        tag = "Est")

dep.stack.pred <- inla.stack(data = list(Y = NA),

                             A = list(A.pred, 1),

                             effects = list(c(s.index, list (Intercept = 1)),

                                            list(A = validation$A,

                                                 B = validation$B,

                                                 C = validation$C,

                                                 D = validation$D,

                                                 E = validation$E)),

                             tag = "Valid")

join.stack <- inla.stack(dep.stack, dep.stack.pred)

U <- 0.01

hyper.prec <- list(theta = list (

  prior = "pc.prec",

  param = c(U, 0.05)))

form <- Y ~ -1 + Intercept + A + B + C +

  f(spatial.field2, model = spde1) +  f(D, model = "rw2", hyper = hyper.prec) +                     f(E, model = "iid")

Model   <- inla(form,

                   data = inla.stack.data(join.stack, spde = spde1),

                   family = "nbinomial",

                   inla.setOption(scale.model.default = TRUE),

                   inla.mode = "experimental",

                   control.inla = list(tolerance = 1e-10),

                   control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(join.stack), compute = T, link=1))

#Make summary of predicted versus observed

index.test_CR <- inla.stack.index(join.stack, 'Valid')$data

summary(index.test_CR1)

summary(test_steps$Y)

#Calculate correlation between predicted and observed

cor(index.test_CR1, test_steps$Y)

messages.body_plain:
﻿
The﻿ linear predictor quantity (eta) and version transformed via the link function, typically controls the location parameter of the data distribution, so is never directly comparable to observations (y) without taking in account the variance and/or full distribution model.
Credible intervals (like confidence intervals) for eta do not incorporate the variability of the observations themselves; for that you need to take the full distribution into account, e.g. through predictive intervals on the data level itself. This is an extremely fundamental thing, but it appears this is not handled properly in teaching materials about regression and hierarchical models, since we see this confusion a lot.

That’s why a common recommendation is to sample from the observation distribution conditionally on samples of the posterior for eta; it gives a Monte Carlo approximation of the distribution for each left out observation. For specific models one can often compute quantities more directly, e.g. instead of sampling y, use the sampled eta values to approximate the resulting mixture distribution pdf or pdf instead.
In the online inlabru package examples, we use that technique to estimate a predictive mixture of Poisson distributions, but direct sampling is simpler, and works the same for all models.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
As a further example, we can consider the overall variance of the left out observations, using the “tower property” of expectations:
For expectations,
E(y)=E(E(y|eta)),
so that the overall average is the average of the conditional expectations.
But for variances, this turns into two terms,
Var(y) = E(Var(y|eta)) + Var(E(y|eta)),
so that the variance is the average of the conditional variances, plus the variance of the conditional expectations. For regression models, the whole point is usually that eta is different for each observation  (and typically E(y|eta) = g^-1(eta) from the inverse link function) so both terms contribute to the overall variance of the observations.

Finn

On Saturday, December 11, 2021 at 4:30:01 PM UTC-5 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
> As a further example, we can consider the overall variance of the left out observations, using the “tower property” of expectations:
> For expectations,
> E(y)=E(E(y|eta)),
> so that the overall average is the average of the conditional expectations.
> But for variances, this turns into two terms,
> Var(y) = E(Var(y|eta)) + Var(E(y|eta)),
> so that the variance is the average of the conditional variances, plus the variance of the conditional expectations. For regression models, the whole point is usually that eta is different for each observation  (and typically E(y|eta) = g^-1(eta) from the inverse link function) so both terms contribute to the overall variance of the observations.
>
> Finn
>
> > On 11 Dec 2021, at 21:14, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > ﻿
> > ﻿
> > ﻿
> > The﻿ linear predictor quantity (eta) and version transformed via the link function, typically controls the location parameter of the data distribution, so is never directly comparable to observations (y) without taking in account the variance and/or full distribution model.
> > Credible intervals (like confidence intervals) for eta do not incorporate the variability of the observations themselves; for that you need to take the full distribution into account, e.g. through predictive intervals on the data level itself. This is an extremely fundamental thing, but it appears this is not handled properly in teaching materials about regression and hierarchical models, since we see this confusion a lot.
> >
> > That’s why a common recommendation is to sample from the observation distribution conditionally on samples of the posterior for eta; it gives a Monte Carlo approximation of the distribution for each left out observation. For specific models one can often compute quantities more directly, e.g. instead of sampling y, use the sampled eta values to approximate the resulting mixture distribution pdf or pdf instead.
> > In the online inlabru package examples, we use that technique to estimate a predictive mixture of Poisson distributions, but direct sampling is simpler, and works the same for all models.

messages.body_plain:
The code ran well. Thank you all for this great technical support, this was really really helpful.

Here is my code in case someone wants to scrap some pieces of it.  I used a homemade package Bidart and reprocessed data from https://spatial-analyst.net/book/NGS8HMC , nonetheless some parts may come in handy.
Before you run the code make sure that :
R version is up to date (in R 3.6 the RAM cost was much higher)
the computer has plenty of RAM if you are using several cores (I had to set up a 100 G swap file)
as said by Håvard the number of parameters is lower than 52, else be using empirical Bayes

#############
# load data #
#############

train_data_set = readRDS("Heavy_metals_comparison/validation_train.RDS")
coords = train_data_set$train_locs

#################
# get inla mesh #
#################

lonlat_CRS = sp::CRS("+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84 +no_defs +ellps=WGS84 +towgs84=0,0,0")
prdomain <- INLA::inla.nonconvex.hull(points = coords, convex = -0.03, concave = -0.05,
                                  resolution=c(100,100), crs = lonlat_CRS)
prmesh <- INLA::inla.mesh.2d(boundary=prdomain, max.edge=c(.45,1),
                         cutoff=0.2, crs = lonlat_CRS)
warnings()
# I get waring whrn I put crs
plot(prmesh$loc, pch = 16, cex = .1)

###################################################
# get environmental covariates at INLA mesh nodes #
###################################################

# loqd environmental covariates
load(file = "Heavy_metals/NGS8HMC.Rdata")
grid.list <- c("dairp.asc", "dmino.asc", "dquksig.asc", "dTRI.asc", "gcarb.asc",
               "geomap.asc", "globedem.asc", "minotype.asc", "nlights03.asc", "sdroads.asc",
               "twi.asc", "vsky.asc", "winde.asc", "glwd31.asc")
gridmaps <- rgdal::readGDAL("Heavy_metals/usgrids5km/dairp.asc")
names(gridmaps)[1] <- sub(".asc", "", grid.list[1])
for(i in grid.list[-1]) {
  gridmaps@data[sub(".asc", "", i[1])] <- rgdal::readGDAL(paste("Heavy_metals/usgrids5km/",i, sep = ""))$band1
}
# projection of environmental covariates
AEA <- "+proj=aea +lat_1=29.5 +lat_2=45.5 +lat_0=23 +lon_0=-96 +x_0=0 +y_0=0
+ellps=GRS80 +datum=NAD83 +units=m +no_defs"
sp::proj4string(gridmaps) = sp::CRS(AEA)

# put INLA nodes in same CRS as environmental covariates
INLA_locs = data.frame(prmesh$loc[,-3])
INLA_nodes_data <- sp::SpatialPointsDataFrame(coords = INLA_locs[,c(1, 2)], data = INLA_locs,
                               proj4string = lonlat_CRS)
INLA_nodes_data_AEA = sp::spTransform(INLA_nodes_data, AEA)

# overlay environemntal covariates grid on INLA nodes
X_locs_INLA = sp::over(INLA_nodes_data_AEA, gridmaps)

###############################
# imputation of missing nodes #
###############################

par(mfrow = c(2, 1))

Bidart::plot_pointillist_painting(
  INLA_locs[!is.na <http://is.na>(X_locs_INLA$twi),c(1,2)],
  X_locs_INLA$twi[!is.na <http://is.na>(X_locs_INLA$twi)],
  main = "observed and unobserved twi"
)
points(INLA_locs[is.na <http://is.na>(X_locs_INLA$twi),c(1,2)], pch = 16)
maps::map("state", add = T)

X_locs_INLA$twi[is.na <http://is.na>(X_locs_INLA$twi)] = mean(X_locs_INLA$twi, na.rm = T)
Bidart::plot_pointillist_painting(
  INLA_locs,
  X_locs_INLA$twi,
  main = "observed and imputed twi"
)
points(INLA_locs[is.na <http://is.na>(X_locs_INLA$twi),c(1,2)], pch = 16)
maps::map("state", add = T)

Bidart::plot_pointillist_painting(
  INLA_locs[!is.na <http://is.na>(X_locs_INLA$gcarb),c(1,2)],
  X_locs_INLA$gcarb[!is.na <http://is.na>(X_locs_INLA$gcarb)],
  main = "observed and unobserved gcarb"
)
points(INLA_locs[is.na <http://is.na>(X_locs_INLA$gcarb),c(1,2)], pch = 16)
maps::map("state", add = T)

X_locs_INLA$gcarb[is.na <http://is.na>(X_locs_INLA$gcarb)] = mean(X_locs_INLA$gcarb, na.rm = T)
Bidart::plot_pointillist_painting(
  INLA_locs,
  X_locs_INLA$gcarb,
  main = "observed and imputed gcarb"
)
maps::map("state", add = T)

X_locs_INLA$globedem = X_locs_INLA$globedem * (X_locs_INLA$globedem>0)
Bidart::plot_pointillist_painting(
  INLA_locs[!is.na <http://is.na>(X_locs_INLA$globedem),c(1,2)],
  X_locs_INLA$globedem[!is.na <http://is.na>(X_locs_INLA$globedem)],
  main = "observed and unobserved globedem"
)
points(INLA_locs[is.na <http://is.na>(X_locs_INLA$globedem),c(1,2)], pch = 16)
maps::map("state", add = T)

X_locs_INLA$globedem[is.na <http://is.na>(X_locs_INLA$globedem)] = 0
Bidart::plot_pointillist_painting(
  INLA_locs,
  X_locs_INLA$globedem,
  main = "observed and imputed globedem"
)
maps::map("state", add = T)

# creating evironmental covariates vector
X_range_env_INLA = do.call(cbind, list(X_locs_INLA$globedem, X_locs_INLA$twi, X_locs_INLA$gcarb))

#####################
# scaling INLA data #
#####################
apply(X_range_env_INLA, 2, mean)
apply(X_range_env_INLA, 2, sd)

processed_data = readRDS("Heavy_metals_comparison/processed_data.RDS")
X_range_env_INLA = X_range_env_INLA - tcrossprod(rep(1, nrow(X_range_env_INLA)), processed_data$X_locs_mean[c("globedem", "twi", "gcarb")])
X_range_env_INLA = X_range_env_INLA %*% diag(1/processed_data$X_locs_sd[c("globedem", "twi", "gcarb")])
apply(X_range_env_INLA, 2, mean)
apply(X_range_env_INLA, 2, sd)

#######################
# precicting KL basis #
#######################

KL_basis_for_INLA = Bidart::predict_KL_basis(
  KL_basis = train_data_set$train_KL_decomposition,
  predicted_locs = prmesh$loc[,c(1,2)],
  seed =1)
dev.off()
par(mfrow = c(2,2))
Bidart::plot_pointillist_painting(prmesh$loc[,c(1,2)], KL_basis_for_INLA[,1])
maps::map("state", add = T)
Bidart::plot_pointillist_painting(prmesh$loc[,c(1,2)], KL_basis_for_INLA[,2])
maps::map("state", add = T)
Bidart::plot_pointillist_painting(prmesh$loc[,c(1,2)], KL_basis_for_INLA[,3])
maps::map("state", add = T)
Bidart::plot_pointillist_painting(prmesh$loc[,c(1,2)], KL_basis_for_INLA[,4])
maps::map("state", add = T)

#############################
# making A matrix and SPDEs #
#############################

n_spatial_basis = 25 # number of spatial basis function covariates
# that will go into the SPDEs

  ##########################################
  # nonsationary spatially coherent effect #
  ##########################################

messages.body_plain:
Hi Shauhin,

the rw1 process is non-differentiable, so it would only make sense to do this with e.g. rw2 models, where the derivative is well defined.
Even though the posterior mean might look smooth, the joint distribution reveals that the realisations themselves aren't, and if you were to compute the finite difference "derivative estimate" posteriors you'd see that their variance will go to infinity the shorter the delta-value is.  This is in stark contrast to frequentist penalised spline point estimates, that have more in common with the posterior mean (or mode) than the actual posterior process distributions.

That said, you can use the same approach as in other systems (if you have rw2 models). Likely easiest to use posterior sampling with inla.posterior.sample and calculate the finite differences for each sampled process.

Finn

you only need to define a precision for one of the terms, as the other
one is scaled automatically (like with scale.model=TRUE argument),

so with this one

> > As a further example, we can consider the overall variance of the
> > left out observations, using the “tower property” of expectations:
> > For expectations,
> > E(y)=E(E(y|eta)),
> > so that the overall average is the average of the conditional
> > expectations.
> > But for variances, this turns into two terms,
> > Var(y) = E(Var(y|eta)) + Var(E(y|eta)),
> > so that the variance is the average of the conditional variances,
> > plus the variance of the conditional expectations. For regression
> > models, the whole point is usually that eta is different for each
> > observation  (and typically E(y|eta) = g^-1(eta) from the inverse
> > link function) so both terms contribute to the overall variance of
> > the observations.
> >
> > Finn
> >
> > > On 11 Dec 2021, at 21:14, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com>
> > > wrote:
> > >
> > > ﻿
> > > ﻿
> > > ﻿
> > > The﻿ linear predictor quantity (eta) and version transformed via
> > > the link function, typically controls the location parameter of
> > > the data distribution, so is never directly comparable to
> > > observations (y) without taking in account the variance and/or
> > > full distribution model.
> > > Credible intervals (like confidence intervals) for eta do not
> > > incorporate the variability of the observations themselves; for
> > > that you need to take the full distribution into account, e.g.
> > > through predictive intervals on the data level itself. This is an
> > > extremely fundamental thing, but it appears this is not handled
> > > properly in teaching materials about regression and hierarchical
> > > models, since we see this confusion a lot.
> > >
> > > That’s why a common recommendation is to sample from the
> > > observation distribution conditionally on samples of the posterior
> > > for eta; it gives a Monte Carlo approximation of the distribution
> > > for each left out observation. For specific models one can often
> > > compute quantities more directly, e.g. instead of sampling y, use
> > > the sampled eta values to approximate the resulting mixture
> > > distribution pdf or pdf instead.
> > > In the online inlabru package examples, we use that technique to
> > > estimate a predictive mixture of Poisson distributions, but direct
> > > sampling is simpler, and works the same for all models.
> > >
> > > Finn

> > > > in this new approach to quantile regression we try to associate the linear predictor to the quantile, so that we explicitely model the quantile as in standard quantile regression, and then map the quantile to the canonical parameter of the distribution, so that basically estimating the quantile results in simply estimating a transformation of the canonical parameter of the distribution.
> > > >
> > > > The mapping step is then just a reparametrization of the Poisson, in order to include the linear predictor defined on the quantile. Basically what we are trying to do there is to write the mean lambda as a function of the quantile of level alpha, which in turn can be written in terms of linar predictor.
> > > >
> > > > In the case of the Continuous Poisson, you have that the quantile of level alpha is defined as Q_alpha = IRGamma(lambda, alpha), where the IRGamma is the incomplete regularized gamma function, of parameters lambda and alpha. In practice then, if you want to write lambda as a function of Q_alpha, you simply have to invert that relationship, which is why you have the \Gamma^{-1}. The reparametrization thus consists of expressing lambda as the inverse of an incomplete regularized gamma function.

messages.subject_clean: quantile regression with negative binomial distribution for overdispersed count data
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA users,

I asked this question in another thread related to quantile regression, but maybe it deserves its own separate thread.

I am really interested in the idea of "model-aware quantile regression", and have been experimenting with INLA for that topic. My research uses negative binomial regression a lot because I am dealing with overdispersed count data. But I realized that most of the existing examples or demos of model-aware quantile regression using INLA are based on Poisson regression.

Specifically, I checked out Tullia's toy demo on this under this link: https://github.com/tulliapadellini/INLA-quantreg
I was able to replicate it and also applied it to my own count data. But I keep getting error messages when I change the distribution family from "poisson" to "nbinomial".
The error message is  "inla.mkl: src/inla.c:17794: inla_parse_data: Assertion `0 == 1' failed. Aborted (core dumped)"

I forgot where I read it, but I remembered seeing somewhere that says INLA allows the quantile option for poisson, negative binomial as well as binomial distribution. It didn't return error messages when I changed it to "binomial", but it somehow didn't work for "nbinomial".

My question is:
 Is this because the quantile option for negative binomial distribution is not yet supported in INLA? Or is this caused by some other bug either on my side or on INLA's side?
Also, if it is not yet supported, does anyone have any idea how I could estimate a negative binomial quantile regression using the existing framework?
Thank you!

ruilin

Yes, the code can be applied to other datasets with the same options, just make sure the priors match the scale of the parameters fitted because with small samples, they can have an important impact on your results. Here the standardized Gaussian suits fine.  Model 5 is using family="coxph" if you look carefully. The only difference with model 4 is that I define a smooth spline for the baseline hazard function because it is less prone to overfit the observed data compared to the piecewise linear default function, you should keep it for your application to other datasets.

Best,
Denis Rustand

messages.body_plain:
I checked the code and the quantile for nbinomial is not yet
implemented. I'm a bit reluctant about the neg.binomial as its
essentially just a poisson  with an iid normal random effect (well,
techically its a log of a Gamma(a,a) distribution, but they are more or
less the same). so the question is if Poisson is the correct choice even
for nbinomial.

I'm happy you like the idea of the model-aware q-regression. from the
response we got about this work, very few seems to understand/appriciate
it.

Best
Håvard

> Dear INLA users,

> I asked this question in another thread related to quantile

>
> I am really interested in the idea of "model-aware quantile
> regression", and have been experimenting with INLA for that topic. My
> research uses negative binomial regression a lot because I am dealing
> with overdispersed count data. But I realized that most of the
> existing examples or demos of model-aware quantile regression using

> Specifically, I checked out Tullia's toy demo on this under this
> link: https://github.com/tulliapadellini/INLA-quantreg

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] mlik to calculate Bayes factor
messages.body_plain:
its discussed in the JRSSB 2009 paper.

and the approximation of \pi(\theta| y)  we use is from the 'new
features' paper, and by integrating this approximation this is what
gives the marginal likelihood estimate ``integration''

> inla(y~1,data=data.frame(y=0))$mlik
                                                 [,1]
log marginal-likelihood (integration) -0.001348612533
log marginal-likelihood (Gaussian)    -0.081220457277

whereas the 'Gaussian' is just treating \pi(\theta | y) as Gaussian,
which is classical ``estimating marginal likelihood using laplace
approximation'' approach.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] unexpected intra-variant variances estimation in disaggregation spatial regression model using INLA()
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] unexpected intra-variant variances estimation in disaggregation spatial regression model using INLA()
messages.body_plain:
Thanks so much! It is so nice that you have answered.

Yes, I did two interesting experiments. The first one is that I used an arbitrarily chosen simple normal nugget effect (N(0, sigma)) to generate one single 100*100 grid realization, without intercept and any covariates, just the nugget effect (N(0, sigma)). Then, I averaged those 100*100 grids to 10*10 coarser averaged areal value, use INLA() to function to fit those coarser 10*10 averaged areal values. Even for this one single realization, the precision for the gaussian observation is 1/100 times the sigma of the finer resolution (100*100) nugget variance that I arbitrarily chose in the first place. This is aligned with a perfect world without any spatial random fields or SPDE model or numerical representation involved.

However, if I added a Matérn covariance spatial random field in the simulation model, plus a simple intercept and a simple normal nugget effect like above, and fit the model on the composite averaged observations. The INLA() function cannot give accurate precision for the observation value for the averaged coarser areal observations (very different from 1/100 times the fine resolution nugget variance, which is expected). Thus, I am wondering if it is caused by the interaction with the numerical representation of the spatial random field itself, since the INLA() function can derive a good estimation on the pure composite nugget effects without any spatial random fields involved. Looking forward to your reply!

Thanks,
Bowen

> So in a perfect world your nugget variance estimate should be 1/100 times the fine resolution nugget variance.
> In practice, it will likely differ from that due to interaction with the numerical representation of the random field itself, and due to non-identifiability of the covariance parameters (with only a single field realisation, the parameters are not fully identifiable).

Then, I averaged 100 grids to one polygon, resulting  10*10 polygons as coarser observations. The goal is to predict the 10000 underlying grids level data when only observing those coarser a100 real/polygon observations. While INLA() can reveal the kappa, marignal variances of the Matérn covariance function as well as the intercept with a reasonable accuracy, the nugget effect sigmae is way off from the true value. messages.body_plain:
It is extremely likely that the model simply isn't identifiable. Even a model with _only_ a Matern field and no nugget has non-identifiable covariance parameters (only the variance of the driving noise process is consistently estimable under infill asymptotics) when only a single realisation is available.  It is therefore quite possible that INLA has actually computed an accurate estimate of the true posterior distribution for the problem presented to it, and that that posterior distribution isn't as close to the true parameter values as one might want it to be.

Finn

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] unexpected intra-variant variances estimation in disaggregation spatial regression model using INLA()
messages.body_plain:
Thank you so much for your explanation.
Yes, it helps a lot to understand this phenomenon.

Another interesting thing I found that is INLA() function can derive a very good estimation for all the covariance parameters (marginal variance for the process, scale/range) associated with the Matern field as well as the nugget effect's sigma^2 value even one realization is available under the condition that the original 100*100 finer grids values are input as observational values in the function, not the 10*10 coarser areal observational values. When the 10*10 coarser areal values that are averaged from the original finer grids values are used as input as observational values in the function, the INLA() function can also derive good estimation for all the covariance parameters (marginal variance for the process, scale/range) associated with Matern field, however, the nugget effect's sigma is off from the expected one (1/100 times the fine resolution nugget variance). Thus, in the context of the areal interpolation process which is to derive the original model parameters from coarser averaged composite observations (lower resolution to predict higher resolution), the model seems still able to derive the covariance parameters for a reasonable precision but only lose the ability to derive the nugget variances (precision for the gaussian observations). I am wondering what could be the possible reason for the INLA() function to lose the ability to reveal the underlying true nugget variances only in the context of the areal interpolation process using a single realization. Your thoughts would be extremely helpful! Thanks!

Best,
Bowen

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

> Could you please clarify for me some points regarding that example? In particular, do the Figures 6 and 7 represent the overall effect of the main predictor on the response variable, as well as for each individual, respectively?

Figure 4.6 is placed right after the model with fixed effect and subject iid effects, which is unfortunate, because Figure 4.6 shows the estimates from a different model. Figure 4.7 shows a summary of the model fit that includes random slopes. Here, in order to represent the line, the posterior mean of the intercept and subject-slop are used.

> Or do these Figures represent something a little bit different than what I am looking for? I am a little bit confused on that, because the description of the Figure 6 says “this model assumes the same slope of the effect of Days on the students”, but all 16 graphs of the Figure 6 show different slopes.

Yes. AS I said, the placement of the figure is unfortunate. I may change this in the book so that this Firme is shown a bit earlier in the text. In the printed version I guess this is not an issue. Also, please check the R code of the  book. Therein you will see how each figure is produced and you will get a better understanding of what is being plotted.

Best,

Virgilio

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Thanks for your reply!

I apologize for the miscommunications in the previous question. I summarized two experiments here:
(1)  A very simple model with nugget effects only (variance of the only driving noise process). The INLA() function can reveal the true/appropriate nugget variances value in both the original 100*100 grid's value as observations and the composite averaged 10*10 coarser areal values as observations. If the original 100*100 grids simulation values are input to the INLA() function as observations, true nugget variances sigma^2 can be revealed and if the 10*10 composite averaged areal values are input to the INLA() function as observations, 1/100 times the true sigma^2 that I chose for simulating the finer grids value can also be successfully revealed. This simple nugget effect variance-only model is consistently estimable when a single realization is available.

(2) Matern random field involved spatial model. The INLA() function can reveal a good estimation for all the covariance parameters (marginal variance for the process, scale/range) associated with the Matern field as well as the nugget effect's variance value when only one realization is available only when the original 100*100 finer grids values are input as observational values in the function. If the composite averaged areal values like 10*10 composite averaged areal values are input to the function as observations, the INLA() cannot derive the supposed 1/100 times the finer scale nugget effect sigma^2 value but all the other Matern covariance parameters.

Thus, I am wondering why the INLA() function can successfully derive all the model parameters including the true nugget effect variance when observing the finer resolution grids value. However, the function failed to derive the 1/100 times the finer resolution nugget effect variance (precision for the gaussian observation calculated in this case is very different from 1/100 times the original nugget effect variance for finer grids) when observing aggregated scale values but still capable of deriving a good estimate for all the other Matern covariance parameters? Thanks!

Thanks,
Bowen

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I've seen that the use of the Tweedie distribution is becoming more and more common in different R packages. I wonder whether there's been some sort of development that makes the Tweedie somehow more stable.

I agree with James Thorson and Chris.  A continuous ZIM similar to the zeroinflatedpoisson/nbinomial2 would be an invaluable addition to model many ecological processes. It allows to link the probability of presence and the abundance in zero inflated continuous datasets. Delta model or hurdle models can be particularly annoying due to their independence.

Best,
iosu
